intro: Seven documented cases where one of the patterns showed up in published research on a real system or benchmark. Each summary reports what the source says and no more. Each links to the primary source, and each was checked against that source's abstract or full text.
note: These cases show a pattern occurring. They do not show that the system, the research group, or the organization involved is bad. Studying how a system behaves under evaluation is how the field improves.

cases.title: Private variants on a public leaderboard
cases.what: Singh et al. (2025) studied Chatbot Arena, a public leaderboard that ranks models by votes from users. They report that some providers could test several model variants privately before release and choose which scores to publish. The most extreme case they identify is Meta, which tested 27 private variants before the Llama 4 release. They also estimate that Google and OpenAI received about 19.2% and 20.4% of all Arena test prompts, while 83 open-weight models together received about 29.7%. In a controlled experiment, adding Arena-style training data raised a model's score on an Arena-derived test set by up to 112% in relative terms, while a broader benchmark (MMLU) did not improve.
cases.check: Ask how many variants were tried before the reported one, and whether the score was confirmed on a second measure that nobody optimized. A published result should say how many candidates it was selected from.

source.label: Singh et al. (2025), The Leaderboard Illusion, arXiv:2504.20879

cases.title: Fresh grade-school math problems, lower scores
cases.what: Zhang et al. (2024) wrote GSM1k, a new set of grade-school math problems built to match the popular GSM8K benchmark in style and difficulty. Some model families scored up to 8% lower on GSM1k than on GSM8K. Models that were more likely to generate GSM8K examples verbatim showed bigger gaps (Spearman's r² = 0.36), which the authors take to suggest partial memorization. They also report that many frontier models showed minimal overfitting, so the gap was not universal.
cases.check: Build a small private set of look-alike items that has never been posted online, and compare scores on public and private items. A large gap is the warning sign; no gap is a reasonable reassurance.

source.label: Zhang et al. (2024), A careful examination of large language model performance on grade school arithmetic, arXiv:2405.00332

cases.title: A screening tool in eleven clinics
cases.what: Beede et al. (2020) studied a deep learning system for detecting diabetic eye disease that was used in eleven clinics in Thailand. Through interviews and observation they found that several socio-environmental factors affected model performance, nursing workflows, and the patient experience. They describe a tension between the data quality the model required and the data quality that an imperfect, resource-constrained clinic could produce. They argue that this kind of human-centered study should accompany prospective tests of accuracy.
cases.check: Before scaling, pilot in a few real sites and watch the system in use. Measure the workflow (time, rejected inputs, handoffs), not only the model's accuracy on clean validation data.

source.label: Beede et al. (2020), A human-centered evaluation of a deep learning system deployed in clinics for the detection of diabetic retinopathy, CHI 2020

cases.title: Succeeds once, fails the next time
cases.what: Yao et al. introduced τ-bench, which simulates conversations between a user and an agent that has tools and policies to follow. They report that even state-of-the-art function-calling agents such as gpt-4o succeed on fewer than 50% of tasks. They also propose pass^k, which measures reliability across multiple attempts at the same task, and report that pass^8 is below 25% in the retail domain.
cases.check: Run every test case several times and report the all-runs-pass rate next to the average. A single run per item cannot show whether a success was repeatable.

source.label: Yao et al. (2025), τ-bench, ICLR 2025, arXiv:2406.12045

cases.title: A widely used sepsis model, validated locally
cases.what: Wong et al. (2021) externally validated the Epic Sepsis Model, a proprietary tool in use at many US hospitals, on 38,455 hospitalizations at Michigan Medicine, where sepsis occurred in about 7%. They report a hospitalization-level AUC of 0.63, that the model did not identify about 67% of patients with sepsis, and that it generated alerts for about 18% of all hospitalized patients. They conclude that it has poor discrimination and calibration.
cases.check: Validate on your own site's data, with the metrics and alert threshold fixed in advance, before relying on a vendor's reported performance. Count the alert burden as well as the hits.

source.label: Wong et al. (2021), External validation of a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model in hospitalized patients, JAMA Internal Medicine 181(8)

cases.title: One accuracy number, three commercial classifiers
cases.what: Buolamwini and Gebru (2018) found that two common face-analysis benchmarks were heavily weighted toward lighter-skinned subjects (79.6% and 86.2%). They built a dataset balanced by gender and skin type and tested three commercial gender classification systems on it. Error rates were up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women, against a maximum of 0.8% for lighter-skinned men.
cases.check: Define the groups that matter before looking at the overall score, report results for each, and show the worst one next to the average. Make sure each group has enough examples to carry its own error bars.

cases.title: Hundreds of covid-19 prediction models, reviewed
cases.what: Wynants et al. (2020) ran a living systematic review of prediction models for diagnosing and predicting the course of covid-19. In its first version it rated all included studies at high risk of bias; later updates, covering many more models, reported that nearly all were poorly reported and at high risk of bias. For the first version, the authors attributed this mainly to non-representative selection of control patients, exclusion of patients who had not yet had the outcome, and a high risk of overfitting. They conclude that the reported performance is probably optimistic.
cases.check: Ask whether the data represent the people the model will be used on, whether the model was tested on a cohort it was not built from, and whether the report is complete enough to rerun and audit.

source.label: Wynants et al. (2020), Prediction models for diagnosis and prognosis of covid-19: systematic review and critical appraisal, BMJ 369:m1328
